title: Acharei Mot: live by them (Leviticus 18:5)
hookLine: "which if a man do, he shall live by them"; so saving a life overrides almost every law (Yoma 85b)

cards: It's Saturday morning in an observant neighborhood. A man who wouldn't turn on a light switch on Shabbat, who walks to synagogue in the rain rather than drive, sees his neighbor collapse on the sidewalk.
He pulls out his phone, calls an ambulance, and does everything the dispatcher tells him. Nobody who knows Jewish law would blink; they'd say he did exactly what the law requires.
The reason goes back to a few words in Leviticus 18, and to a rabbi who read them very carefully.

teach.b: In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, God's statutes and ordinances are the ones "which if a man do, he shall live by them." In the Talmud, the sages ask where we learn that saving a life overrides Shabbat.

teach.h: SAMUEL: AND NOT DIE BY THEM.
teach.b: Several answers are offered, and the one left standing is Samuel's: he shall live by them, and not die by them. The commandments are for living. If keeping one would cost a life, the life comes first.
Jewish law calls this pikuach nefesh. Nefesh is a life, a soul.

Pikuach comes from a picture in the Mishnah: rubble falls on someone on Shabbat, and you don't know whether they're under it, or alive. You clear the rubble anyway. That clearing, uncovering, is pikuach.
Even a doubt about danger to life is enough.

teach.h: THREE LIMITS, AND A LONG REACH.
teach.b: There are limits. The Talmud names three things a person may not do even to save their own life: worship idols, commit murder, or commit certain forbidden sexual acts. Almost everything else gives way.
Fasting on Yom Kippur, Shabbat, the food laws: a sick person may be required to set them aside. And the idea reaches into ordinary days.
Maimonides counts keeping your body healthy as part of serving God, because you can't do much of anything if you're broken.
Live by them, not in spite of them.

how: Jewish law requires setting aside Shabbat, fasts and most other commandments to save a life or treat serious illness; observant doctors, nurses and volunteer ambulance crews work on Shabbat for this reason.

o: the soul's journey after a person has died
saving a life, which overrides almost every law
keeping Shabbat strictly, even in an emergency

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: live by them, not die by them

s: calling an ambulance on Shabbat breaks Jewish law
pikuach nefesh requires it. saving a life overrides Shabbat.
even a doubt about danger to life is enough
the Mishnah says clear the rubble even if you're not sure anyone's there.
saving a life overrides absolutely every law
the Talmud names three exceptions: idolatry, murder and forbidden relations.

games.q: it's Shabbat. a wall collapses, and someone may be under the rubble. you're not sure. what does the Mishnah say?
o: only dig if you're sure someone's there.
games.why: clear it now, even on a doubt. that act of uncovering gives the principle its name: pikuach nefesh.

practice: Notice your body: where is it tired, tight, ignored?
Think of when you last drank water, ate properly, slept enough, walked outside, saw a doctor about the thing you keep putting off, and let one small thing your body needs come to mind.
Not as self-improvement; as taking care of a life.

wordCard.voice: Pikuach nefesh. Saving a life: the principle, drawn from live by them, that protecting life overrides almost every other commandment.

orig.note: Hebrew: saving a life; literally uncovering a soul, from clearing rubble off someone.

carryVoice: Your line: live by them. The commandments are for living. Four hundred nine days in.
